lead_headline: Arvada Council Eyes 18-Month Data Center Moratorium to Fill Code Gaps

type_specific.meeting_summary: Arvada City Council held a study session on August 11, 2026, to learn about data centers — what they are, how they are categorized by size and power demand, where they exist in Colorado, and how other municipalities have responded. Staff presented a recommendation for an 18-month moratorium on new data center applications, explaining that current land-use codes lack adequate definitions and that infrastructure capacity questions around water, energy, and fiber have not been analyzed. Council discussed how to craft the moratorium to avoid inadvertently blocking smaller, ancillary uses such as cell towers, hospital campuses, and government facilities, and directed staff to proceed with an 18-month moratorium focused on primary-use data centers with explicit carve-outs for those ancillary uses.

briefings.topic: Data Center Overview, Colorado Landscape & Moratorium Recommendation
briefings.presenter_name: Kelsey (last name not given), Candace (last name not given), Rob (last name not given), and Jessica Garner
briefings.presenter_role: City staff, Arvada Community Development / Planning (specific titles not stated in transcript)
prose_paragraphs: Staff opened by framing data centers as a rapidly evolving national and local issue, noting that numerous Colorado municipalities are already imposing moratoriums ranging from six to 18 months — with the Town of Lochbuie recently adopting an unusually long five-year moratorium in direct response to a large facility proposed in Weld County. Staff explained that the Colorado state legislature considered two opposing bills this session — one to incentivize data centers and one to restrict them — and both failed to advance, leaving municipalities to act independently. The presentation introduced four size categories used by the Colorado Municipal League: edge/micro (500–5,000 sq ft, 0.5–1 MW), enterprise/internal (20,000–100,000 sq ft, 1–10 MW), regional/colocation (50,000–250,000 sq ft, 10–50 MW), and hyperscale (100,000–2,000,000 sq ft, 75–700+ MW). A map of Colorado's approximately 60 existing data centers showed that none are currently in Arvada, and that most are clustered in urban areas around Centennial and Highlands Ranch. No hyperscale data center has yet been completed in Colorado; the one proposed in Aurora — which did not receive a moratorium at Aurora's most recent council meeting — would be the first.

Staff then walked through Arvada's current Land Development Code (LDC) situation. The city does have an existing definition of 'data center,' but it is broad enough to capture facilities like the CenturyLink central office in Old Town — a legacy telephone switching facility that is not the type of concern driving the moratorium debate. Data centers are currently permitted by conditional use in the Mixed-Use Suburban and Commercial General zone districts (requiring Planning Commission and Council review), and are permitted outright by administrative review in the Industrial Light and Industrial General districts. The only substantive restrictions currently on the books are a 300-foot setback from residential zones and standard municipal noise limits; there are no regulations addressing water consumption, power demand, or building size. Staff emphasized that the ongoing comprehensive plan update — expected to run through approximately October 2027 — presents a timely opportunity to engage the community on data center policy and then translate that input into LDC amendments before any moratorium expires.

Staff's formal recommendation was an 18-month moratorium on new data center applications, citing four primary justifications: state legislative inaction, an outdated and under-defined LDC, strain on the electrical grid, and unquantified water-consumption impacts. Staff noted that utilities staff (Chris Gray and Amy Willihigh) are still conducting infrastructure capacity planning and need time to determine what water demand Arvada can realistically absorb. Council discussion raised concerns about unintentionally blocking small or ancillary data facilities — cell towers, hospital campuses, university systems, and government expansions — and staff confirmed the moratorium ordinance can be drafted to explicitly exclude those uses. By the end of the session, council had coalesced around direction: an 18-month moratorium targeting facilities where data-center operations are the primary use, with explicit carve-outs for cell towers, internet service providers, and ancillary institutional uses, and with no size cap written into the moratorium itself (size and water-use limits to be determined through the comprehensive plan and LDC process).

questions_raised: Does a moratorium freeze all incoming proposals, or can applicants begin site planning while waiting for the moratorium to expire?
Would the proposed moratorium inadvertently block small, ancillary data facilities such as cell towers, hospital campuses, university systems, or government expansions?
Should the moratorium be structured to exclude facilities below a certain size threshold (e.g., under 25–50 megawatts) so that smaller or enterprise-scale users are not blocked?
Could the moratorium be split into a shorter initial phase (e.g., six months) to resolve water-capacity questions, followed by a longer period to complete comprehensive-plan and LDC work?
What water-consumption data does the city currently have on existing facilities — including City Hall — that could serve as a baseline for setting future limits?
Does the Quantum Commons development in unincorporated Jefferson County currently qualify as a data center under any applicable definition, and would annexation bring it under Arvada's moratorium?
Are there examples of data centers that operate entirely or substantially on renewable energy, and could Arvada's future LDC require a minimum renewable-energy percentage?
What tax or use-tax revenue could a regional colocation data center generate for the city given the high value of equipment that cycles on a four-to-seven-year refresh schedule?
Should future LDC provisions include an aggregate cap on total megawatts of data center capacity permitted citywide?
Does Arvada have sufficient industrially zoned land, fiber infrastructure, water supply, and grid capacity to realistically attract even mid-scale regional colocation data centers?
